screens.title: Classic Mode EIGRP Configuration
screens.narratorSegment: Classic mode is the traditional EIGRP configuration where you enable the protocol with router eigrp and an autonomous-system number. In classic mode you typically use network statements that accept an address with an optional wildcard mask. Using a wildcard mask gives you precise control: you can include only the interfaces that should participate in EIGRP. You should always configure no auto-summary in modern networks to avoid classful summarization at boundaries, which can produce unreachable subnets in discontiguous topologies. It is also best practice to set an explicit eigrp router-id; otherwise EIGRP picks the highest loopback or highest active interface IP which can be ambiguous. A common operational step is to make interfaces passive when you do not want Hellos on them, for example to prevent adjacency on user-facing links. In the example shown, you will see a concise, reproducible configuration snippet suitable for a lab. Practice this exact sequence so you can verify neighbor formation and the expected routes using show ip eigrp neighbors and show ip route eigrp. A common misconception is that classful network entries are always safe; they can inadvertently include interfaces and subnets you did not intend to advertise. Verify with show commands.

keyIdea.text: Use network with wildcard masks, no auto-summary, and explicit router-id to keep EIGRP behavior predictable.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Classic Mode
Classic Mode Configuration
Traditional EIGRP with an AS number and network statements that may include wildcard masks.
router eigrp 100
 network 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255
 network 10.0.0.0
 no auto-summary
 eigrp router-id 1.1.1.1
 passive-interface GigabitEthernet0/1
Tip: Wildcard masks give precise control over which interfaces are included in EIGRP. Use them to avoid accidental advertisement.
Common mistake: Relying on classful network statements can enable EIGRP on extra interfaces unexpectedly.
Explanation
  • router eigrp AS starts the EIGRP process for that autonomous-system.
  • network with a wildcard mask lets you target specific interfaces; omit the mask to use classful behavior.
  • no auto-summary prevents unintended aggregation across classful boundaries.
  • passive-interface stops Hellos on links where you do not want neighbors.
Key Takeaway

Classic mode is straightforward and widely deployed; use explicit settings to avoid accidental adjacencies.

screens.title: Named Mode EIGRP and Address Families
screens.narratorSegment: Named mode introduces a named EIGRP instance that encapsulates multiple address families, such as IPv4 and IPv6. The key benefit is clearer separation of process configuration from address-family specifics. In named mode you issue router eigrp with a name, enter an address-family block, set router-id within the AF, and apply ip eigrp on interfaces or use af-interface statements to configure passive behavior. This makes it easier to manage both IPv4 and IPv6 under a single logical instance and helps when migrating from classic mode. Named mode also centralizes topology and policy choices. A practical step when using named mode is to set eigrp router-id explicitly and apply interface-level ip eigrp commands so the interfaces are bound to the AF instance. When migrating, verify that the same AS context is used where required and re-apply any interface authentication and passive settings. A common misconception is that named mode automatically converts existing interface bindings; you must explicitly add ip eigrp to relevant interfaces or use topology and af-interface commands to match prior behavior. Named Mode EIGRP and Address Families means named mode organizes eigrp by address family and simplifies multi-protocol management while requiring explicit interface bindings.. In practical terms, create named instances with address-family separation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Named Mode
Named Mode Configuration
Use a named instance and address-family blocks to separate IPv4 and IPv6 and simplify configuration.
router eigrp MY_EIGRP_INSTANCE
 address-family ipv4 unicast autonomous-system 100
  router-id 1.1.1.1
  interface GigabitEthernet0/0
   ip eigrp 100
  interface Loopback0
   ip eigrp 100
  af-interface GigabitEthernet0/1
   passive-interface
  exit-af-interface
 exit-address-family
Tip: Apply ip eigrp to interfaces so they join the named address-family instance, mirroring classic behavior explicitly.
Why use named mode?
  • Organizes configuration by address family for multi-protocol routers.
  • Makes migration and feature separation easier and less error-prone.
  • Requires explicit interface bindings, which improves clarity.
Key Takeaway

Named mode is more modular and explicit. When migrating, reapply interface-level settings and verify neighbors and routes after the change.

screens.title: Classic vs Named Mode — When and How to Migrate
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between classic and named mode helps you manage modern IOS devices and convert legacy configs correctly. Classic mode ties configuration to the EIGRP process with network statements under router eigrp, while named mode separates the instance name from address-family specifics and uses ip eigrp on interfaces. The practical migration approach is: capture existing classic configuration, create an equivalent named instance, explicitly bind interfaces with ip eigrp, set router-id in the address-family, and reapply any passive-interface, authentication, and summary settings in the new AF context. Always verify neighbors and routes after migration. A common pitfall is assuming interfaces move automatically; they do not. Also confirm that any topology-based settings or keychains are accessible in the named context. For verification, compare show ip eigrp neighbors, show run | section eigrp, and show ip route eigrp before and after the change. Consider performing the migration in maintenance windows and testing one router at a time to avoid transient routing disruptions. The guided example in the lab will walk through migrating a single router from classic to named mode safely. Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Classic vs Named
Feature Comparison
Classic Mode
  • router eigrp with network statements.
  • Interfaces bound implicitly by network entries.
  • Familiar for legacy devices and quick labs.
Named Mode
  • router eigrp with address-family blocks.
  • Interface bindings are explicit using ip eigrp on interfaces.
  • Better for multi-protocol and controlled migrations.
Migration checklist
  1. Export current classic config and note interface bindings and keychains.
  2. Create named instance and address-family; set router-id inside AF.
  3. Apply ip eigrp on each interface and recreate passive/authentication settings.
  4. Verify show ip eigrp neighbors and show ip route eigrp on each router.
Key Takeaway

Make interface bindings and security explicit when moving to named mode, and validate neighbors and routing immediately to catch mistakes.

screens.title: EIGRP Authentication with Key Chains
screens.narratorSegment: Securing EIGRP Hellos and updates is essential. EIGRP supports MD5 authentication using key chains, which must match on both ends of the link. The configuration pattern is to create a key chain with one or more keys and a key-string, then reference that key chain on the interface with ip authentication key-chain eigrp, and set the mode to md5. If the keychain names, key numbers, or key-strings differ between neighbors, adjacencies will fail. When you configure authentication, plan for key rollover by using multiple keys with lifetimes. Common troubleshooting steps include checking show run | section key chain to confirm keychain presence and show ip eigrp neighbors to see whether neighbors form. If authentication is misconfigured, you will see missing neighbor entries and possibly log messages that indicate authentication failures. In lab practice, intentionally breaking the key-string on one side is a useful exercise to observe adjacency loss and then restore connectivity by correcting the keychain. Remember to reapply any keychain references when migrating from classic to named mode, as interface-level bindings must be present in the chosen address-family context.

keyIdea.title: MD5 keychains
keyIdea.text: Key chains must be identical on both neighbors; use interface references and md5 mode to secure EIGRP exchanges.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › EIGRP Authentication
MD5 Authentication
Use key chains and interface authentication to prevent unauthorized adjacencies.
key chain EIGRP_AUTH
 key 1
  key-string MySecurePassword
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip authentication key-chain eigrp 100 EIGRP_AUTH
 ip authentication mode eigrp 100 md5
Tip: Use multiple keys with lifetimes for planned rollover without downtime.
Checklist
  • Keychain name, key numbers, and key-string must match on both neighbors.
  • Apply ip authentication key-chain and ip authentication mode on the interface bound to the EIGRP AS.
  • Verify with show run | section key chain and show ip eigrp neighbors.
Common mistake

A mismatch in the key-string or forgetting to enable md5 mode on the interface will prevent adjacency; check both sides when troubleshooting.

screens.title: Route Summarization and Null0 Behavior
screens.narratorSegment: Route summarization in EIGRP is applied on a per-interface basis using ip summary-address eigrp. When you summarize contiguous subnets into a single advertisement, EIGRP also creates a Null0 route for that summary on the advertising router. That Null0 route prevents routing loops by giving the router a route to discard traffic destined for covered subnets that are not present locally. In practice, you configure summaries on hub interfaces that face other routing domains or spokes, so you reduce the number of routes advertised to neighbors. A practical example is summarizing spoke loopbacks into a larger aggregate on the hub. After you configure the summary, verify on spokes that only the summary appears in their routing table. If you rely on automatic summarization or forget no auto-summary, you may see incorrect advertisements across classful boundaries, causing unreachable destinations. Always test summarization by shutting down a specific subnet on a spoke and observing that the hub still advertises the summary but has the Null0 route to protect against black holes. Summaries are powerful but must be planned to avoid concealing necessary specificity.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Route Summarization
Interface-Level Summarization
Summaries are configured on the interface that advertises to neighbors using ip summary-address eigrp.
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip summary-address eigrp 100 10.0.0.0 255.255.252.0
Note: The router that advertises a summary also installs a Null0 route for that summary to prevent loops if specific subnets disappear.
Verification
- On spokes, use show ip route eigrp to confirm the summary route appears instead of individual subnets.
- On the hub, check the routing table to see the Null0 entry for the summary.
Key Takeaway

Summarization reduces routing table size and contains instability, but confirm Null0 protections and test the summary by simulating a subnet loss.

screens.title: EIGRP Stub Routing
screens.narratorSegment: Stub routing configures a router to behave as an edge device that does not propagate queries into the wider EIGRP domain. Stubs are common in hub-and-spoke topologies where spokes have a single exit to the hub. When configured with eigrp stub followed by keywords like connected and summary, the stub advertises only its connected and summarized routes and will not answer queries from other routers. There are variants such as receive-only, which causes the router to accept updates but advertise nothing. Stub routers reduce C P U and memory usage and prevent query floods toward routers that should not be transit points. To configure, add eigrp stub connected summary under the router process. Verify with show ip eigrp neighbors detail on the hub to see the stub flag set for the neighbor. A common misconception is that stubs isolate networks; they still receive routes from the domain unless configured otherwise — they only restrict what they advertise and whether they propagate queries. Test stub behavior by shutting an interface on the spoke and observing that the hub does not query the stub for alternate paths.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Stub Routing
EIGRP Stub Configuration
Make a router behave as a spoke by limiting what it advertises and by suppressing queries.
router eigrp 100
 eigrp stub connected summary
Why use it: stubs reduce CPU and avoid query storms in hub-and-spoke networks where spokes are not transit routers.
Verification & behavior
  • Use show ip eigrp neighbors detail on hub to confirm stub flag.
  • Stubs advertise connected and summary routes by default when keywords supplied.
  • receive-only makes the router a pure consumer of routes, advertising none.
Key Takeaway

Stubs are a targeted optimization for edge routers; choose the stub keywords based on what routes the spoke must share.

screens.title: Unequal-Cost Load Balancing with Variance
screens.narratorSegment: EIGRP's variance feature enables unequal-cost load balancing by allowing the routing table to accept multiple feasible paths whose metrics are within a factor of the best path. The variance command sets a multiplier; for example variance 2 permits paths with metrics up to best*2 to be installed if they meet the feasibility condition. The feasibility condition is a core requirement: a route must have a reported distance less than the current feasible distance to be considered loop-free and eligible for installation. A practical example from the chapter: if the best path metric is 1000 and you configure variance 2, any feasible path with a metric up to 2000 can be installed. Use variance carefully because it changes load distribution and may affect latency or asymmetric traffic patterns. Monitoring is essential; combine variance with policy or route tagging if needed. variance — Unequal-Cost Load Balancing
Install multiple paths when their metrics are within best*variance and feasibility is satisfied.
Example
Best path metric = 1000. variance 2 -> accepts feasible paths up to metric 2000. Both paths shown will be installed if feasibility condition holds.
Configuration example:

screens.title: Common EIGRP Mistakes and Troubleshooting Checks
screens.narratorSegment: EIGRP adjacencies often fail for a handful of repeatable reasons. Start troubleshooting by confirming autonomous-system numbers match; an AS mismatch prevents neighbor formation entirely. Next, check K-values—if they have been changed from defaults on one router but not another, metric calculation differs and adjacencies break. If you use authentication, verify keychain names, key numbers, and key-strings on both sides and confirm md5 mode is set on the interface. Remember to check that no auto-summary is configured where needed, since automatic summarization can create unreachable subnets. Incorrect network or wildcard entries can enable or disable EIGRP on unintended interfaces; review show run and interface addresses. Interface state problems such as shutdown or incorrect IP addresses and ACLs blocking EIGRP packets are common causes too. Stuck In Active states show a router awaiting replies to a query and indicate connectivity or responsiveness problems; use debug eigrp packets and show ip eigrp topology to locate the missing reply path. The standard verification commands are show ip eigrp neighbors, show ip eigrp topology, show ip route eigrp, and debug eigrp packets. Use them in sequence to isolate configuration, adjacency, or forwarding issues.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Troubleshooting
Common Mistakes
Quick checks that catch most EIGRP problems.
  • AS number mismatch between neighbors.
  • K-value mismatch changing metric calculation.
  • Authentication keychain or mode mismatch.
  • No auto-summary missing or incorrectly applied.
  • Wrong network/wildcard statements or interface down.
  • ACLs blocking EIGRP packets or misconfigured IPs.
If a route is Stuck In Active, it indicates a query was sent but replies were not received; check neighbor reachability and CPU or process stalls on the remote router.
Verification Commands
show ip eigrp neighbors
show ip eigrp topology
show ip route eigrp
debug eigrp packets
Run these in order to confirm adjacency, topology entries, installed EIGRP routes, and live packet-level behavior.
Key Takeaway

Start with AS and authentication checks, then validate interface and ACLs, and finally use show and debug output to find SIA or routing inconsistencies.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity: Implement Summarization and Stub Routing
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity walks through configuring a three-router hub-and-spoke topology. Begin by applying basic IP addressing and then configure EIGRP AS 100 on all routers with no auto-summary and a router-id on each device. On the hub, advertise both spoke subnets and loopback networks. Then configure ip summary-address on the hub interfaces that face each spoke to aggregate the spoke loopbacks into a single summary. On the spoke that should be a stub, add eigrp stub connected summary so it advertises only directly connected and summary routes and does not propagate queries. After making these changes, verify adjacencies using show ip eigrp neighbors. On each spoke, run show ip route eigrp and confirm that the hub is advertising the 10.0.0.0/8 summary instead of individual spoke networks. Finally, simulate failure by shutting down a spoke interface and observe that the hub's Null0 protects the summary. The lab instructions provided in the chapter are reproducible and designed to teach verification and the behavioral changes you should expect. The challenge is to also enable unequal-cost load balancing using variance 3 in the lab and observe route installation behavior.

Activity: Hub-and-Spoke Configuration
Follow these configuration blocks on R1 (Hub), R2 (Spoke1), and R3 (Spoke2).

screens.title: Verification Commands and Interpreting Output
screens.narratorSegment: Verification is the final and essential step after any configuration change. Begin by checking show ip eigrp neighbors to confirm adjacency and to see neighbor uptime and interface information. Next, use show ip eigrp topology to inspect feasible successors, reported distances, and the topology entries that inform the routing table. show ip route eigrp reveals which EIGRP-learned prefixes are installed. If you are troubleshooting authentication or reachability, debug eigrp packets will show packet-level exchanges including MD5 failures when authentication mismatches occur. For stub routers, show ip eigrp neighbors detail on the hub will show a stub flag next to the neighbor entry so you can confirm the spoke is configured correctly. When verifying summarization, look on spokes for the single summary route instead of multiple specific routes and on the hub for the Null0 entry for the summary. If you see Stuck In Active routes in the topology, it indicates queries are unanswered; trace neighbor connectivity and resource utilization on the peer. Combine these commands in sequence to isolate configuration, adjacency, or forwarding problems. Practically, run show commands first, then debug when you need packet-level detail.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Verification
Core Verification Commands
Run these in sequence to validate adjacency, topology, and installed routes.
show ip eigrp neighbors
show ip eigrp topology
show ip route eigrp
debug eigrp packets
Tip: Use show commands first to limit the scope before enabling debug to avoid overwhelming output on production devices.
Interpreting results
- A missing neighbor on show ip eigrp neighbors suggests AS or authentication mismatch, or interface issues.
- Feasible successors listed in topology indicate candidate backup paths; absence may explain why variance did not install a path.
- Stuck In Active in topology hints at missing query replies; trace neighbor reachability and process load.
Key Takeaway

Use the show sequence to narrow the problem, then use debug for packet-level detail when safe. Interpreting topology entries is essential to understand which routes are installed and why.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll move from EIGRP fundamentals to real configuration patterns and enterprise features you will use on the job. We'll cover both classic and named configuration styles so you can read legacy device configs and adopt modern, address-family aware setups. You'll also learn how to secure neighbor exchanges with MD5 keychains, how to reduce routing table growth with interface-level summarization and Null0 protection, and how to limit query floods with stub routers in hub-and-spoke topologies. Finally, we will explain unequal-cost load balancing using variance and the common troubleshooting checks that keep adjacencies healthy. Each topic is presented with concrete command examples, verification steps, and the common mistakes to avoid so you can configure confidently in the lab and on production routers. By the end you'll be able to configure EIGRP on a three-router hub-and-spoke, verify adjacencies and routes, apply summaries on an interface, secure a link with authentication, and explain when to use variance or stub routing. Let's get started with a practical, example-focused approach so configuration becomes second nature.

These first objectives define the hands-on skills you will practice and why they matter. First, you will configure classic EIGRP using the router eigrp autonomous-system command and network statements with wildcard masks so you can enable EIGRP precisely on intended interfaces. Precise network statements prevent accidental adjacency and ensure only correct interfaces run EIGRP. Second, you will configure named-mode EIGRP instances with address-family blocks. Named mode separates the routing process from address-family details, which helps in multi-protocol or IPv6-ready deployments. Third, you will implement MD5 authentication using key chains and interface commands. Authentication prevents unauthorized devices from forming adjacencies and injecting routes. Finally in this screen, you will apply route summarization on interfaces to reduce routing table size and to contain routing instability. Summaries also create a Null0 route that protects against loops when subnets vanish. Each objective is tied to a verification step so you can validate success in the lab and on devices.

These objectives focus on optimizing EIGRP behavior and diagnosing problems. First, you will configure stub routers for hub-and-spoke topologies so edge routers limit their advertised routes and do not propagate queries, reducing load on the hub. Second, you will enable unequal-cost load balancing using the variance command to use additional paths whose metrics are within a factor of the best path, provided they meet the feasibility condition. Third, you will practice common troubleshooting checks such as verifying autonomous-system numbers, K-values, and authentication keychain alignment because mismatches here prevent adjacency. Finally, you will run and interpret key verification commands like show ip eigrp neighbors, show ip eigrp topology, show ip route eigrp, and debug eigrp packets to find issues such as Stuck In Active states or interface problems. Each objective includes a short verification action so you can prove competency during lab work.

Classic mode is the traditional EIGRP configuration where you enable the protocol with router eigrp and an autonomous-system number. In classic mode you typically use network statements that accept an address with an optional wildcard mask. Using a wildcard mask gives you precise control: you can include only the interfaces that should participate in EIGRP. You should always configure no auto-summary in modern networks to avoid classful summarization at boundaries, which can produce unreachable subnets in discontiguous topologies. It is also best practice to set an explicit eigrp router-id; otherwise EIGRP picks the highest loopback or highest active interface IP which can be ambiguous. A common operational step is to make interfaces passive when you do not want Hellos on them, for example to prevent adjacency on user-facing links. In the example shown, you will see a concise, reproducible configuration snippet suitable for a lab. Practice this exact sequence so you can verify neighbor formation and the expected routes using show ip eigrp neighbors and show ip route eigrp. A common misconception is that classful network entries are always safe; they can inadvertently include interfaces and subnets you did not intend to advertise. Verify with show commands.

Named mode introduces a named EIGRP instance that encapsulates multiple address families, such as IPv4 and IPv6. The key benefit is clearer separation of process configuration from address-family specifics. In named mode you issue router eigrp with a name, enter an address-family block, set router-id within the AF, and apply ip eigrp on interfaces or use af-interface statements to configure passive behavior. This makes it easier to manage both IPv4 and IPv6 under a single logical instance and helps when migrating from classic mode. Named mode also centralizes topology and policy choices. A practical step when using named mode is to set eigrp router-id explicitly and apply interface-level ip eigrp commands so the interfaces are bound to the AF instance. When migrating, verify that the same AS context is used where required and re-apply any interface authentication and passive settings. A common misconception is that named mode automatically converts existing interface bindings; you must explicitly add ip eigrp to relevant interfaces or use topology and af-interface commands to match prior behavior. Named Mode EIGRP and Address Families means named mode organizes eigrp by address family and simplifies multi-protocol management while requiring explicit interface bindings.. In practical terms, create named instances with address-family separation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Understanding the difference between classic and named mode helps you manage modern IOS devices and convert legacy configs correctly. Classic mode ties configuration to the EIGRP process with network statements under router eigrp, while named mode separates the instance name from address-family specifics and uses ip eigrp on interfaces. The practical migration approach is: capture existing classic configuration, create an equivalent named instance, explicitly bind interfaces with ip eigrp, set router-id in the address-family, and reapply any passive-interface, authentication, and summary settings in the new AF context. Always verify neighbors and routes after migration. A common pitfall is assuming interfaces move automatically; they do not. Also confirm that any topology-based settings or keychains are accessible in the named context. For verification, compare show ip eigrp neighbors, show run | section eigrp, and show ip route eigrp before and after the change. Consider performing the migration in maintenance windows and testing one router at a time to avoid transient routing disruptions. The guided example in the lab will walk through migrating a single router from classic to named mode safely. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Securing EIGRP Hellos and updates is essential. EIGRP supports MD5 authentication using key chains, which must match on both ends of the link. The configuration pattern is to create a key chain with one or more keys and a key-string, then reference that key chain on the interface with ip authentication key-chain eigrp, and set the mode to md5. If the keychain names, key numbers, or key-strings differ between neighbors, adjacencies will fail. When you configure authentication, plan for key rollover by using multiple keys with lifetimes. Common troubleshooting steps include checking show run | section key chain to confirm keychain presence and show ip eigrp neighbors to see whether neighbors form. If authentication is misconfigured, you will see missing neighbor entries and possibly log messages that indicate authentication failures. In lab practice, intentionally breaking the key-string on one side is a useful exercise to observe adjacency loss and then restore connectivity by correcting the keychain. Remember to reapply any keychain references when migrating from classic to named mode, as interface-level bindings must be present in the chosen address-family context.

Route summarization in EIGRP is applied on a per-interface basis using ip summary-address eigrp. When you summarize contiguous subnets into a single advertisement, EIGRP also creates a Null0 route for that summary on the advertising router. That Null0 route prevents routing loops by giving the router a route to discard traffic destined for covered subnets that are not present locally. In practice, you configure summaries on hub interfaces that face other routing domains or spokes, so you reduce the number of routes advertised to neighbors. A practical example is summarizing spoke loopbacks into a larger aggregate on the hub. After you configure the summary, verify on spokes that only the summary appears in their routing table. If you rely on automatic summarization or forget no auto-summary, you may see incorrect advertisements across classful boundaries, causing unreachable destinations. Always test summarization by shutting down a specific subnet on a spoke and observing that the hub still advertises the summary but has the Null0 route to protect against black holes. Summaries are powerful but must be planned to avoid concealing necessary specificity.

Stub routing configures a router to behave as an edge device that does not propagate queries into the wider EIGRP domain. Stubs are common in hub-and-spoke topologies where spokes have a single exit to the hub. When configured with eigrp stub followed by keywords like connected and summary, the stub advertises only its connected and summarized routes and will not answer queries from other routers. There are variants such as receive-only, which causes the router to accept updates but advertise nothing. Stub routers reduce C P U and memory usage and prevent query floods toward routers that should not be transit points. To configure, add eigrp stub connected summary under the router process. Verify with show ip eigrp neighbors detail on the hub to see the stub flag set for the neighbor. A common misconception is that stubs isolate networks; they still receive routes from the domain unless configured otherwise — they only restrict what they advertise and whether they propagate queries. Test stub behavior by shutting an interface on the spoke and observing that the hub does not query the stub for alternate paths.

After making these changes, verify adjacencies using show ip eigrp neighbors. On each spoke, run show ip route eigrp and confirm that the hub is advertising the 10.0.0.0/8 summary instead of individual spoke networks. Finally, simulate failure by shutting down a spoke interface and observe that the hub's Null0 protects the summary. The lab instructions provided in the chapter are reproducible and designed to teach verification and the behavioral changes you should expect. The challenge is to also enable unequal-cost load balancing using variance 3 in the lab and observe route installation behavior.

Verification is the final and essential step after any configuration change. Begin by checking show ip eigrp neighbors to confirm adjacency and to see neighbor uptime and interface information. Next, use show ip eigrp topology to inspect feasible successors, reported distances, and the topology entries that inform the routing table. show ip route eigrp reveals which EIGRP-learned prefixes are installed. If you are troubleshooting authentication or reachability, debug eigrp packets will show packet-level exchanges including MD5 failures when authentication mismatches occur. For stub routers, show ip eigrp neighbors detail on the hub will show a stub flag next to the neighbor entry so you can confirm the spoke is configured correctly. When verifying summarization, look on spokes for the single summary route instead of multiple specific routes and on the hub for the Null0 entry for the summary. If you see Stuck In Active routes in the topology, it indicates queries are unanswered; trace neighbor connectivity and resource utilization on the peer. Combine these commands in sequence to isolate configuration, adjacency, or forwarding problems. Practically, run show commands first, then debug when you need packet-level detail.

These key concepts are compact reminders of the features you will use regularly. Classic mode uses router eigrp with an AS number and network statements; use wildcard masks for precise interface selection. Named mode uses a router instance name and address-family blocks, requiring explicit ip eigrp bindings on interfaces for IPv4 or IPv6. EIGRP authentication secures Hellos and updates with MD5 key chains applied at the interface level; both sides must match keychain and mode. Keep these definitions in mind as you configure and migrate routers, because the correct combination of instance type, interface binding, and authentication determines whether neighbors will form and routes will be exchanged. Remember to test after each step and use verification commands to confirm behavior. Finish with these operational reminders. Route summarization reduces routing table size and, when applied on an interface, creates a Null0 route on the advertising router to prevent loops. EIGRP stub routing limits what a spoke advertises and prevents it from propagating queries, reducing load in hub-and-spoke networks. Finally, variance enables unequal-cost load balancing by allowing additional paths with metrics up to best*variance provided they meet the feasibility condition; always verify with topology and route displays. Keep these practical points in mind whenever you design or troubleshoot EIGRP deployments: summarize at boundaries, use stubs for edge routers, and control load-sharing with variance while checking feasibility. These patterns will help maintain stability and scalability in enterprise routing domains.
